entries.sentence: The NHS says to check your testicles monthly for changes; a lump or swelling needs a GP visit, and sudden severe pain needs A&E or 999.
entries.note: monthly check; GP for lump/swelling; sudden severe pain A&E/999

entries.sentence: The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower.
entries.note: warm bath; monthly

entries.sentence: A healthy testicle feels smooth and firm, and one being slightly bigger or lower than the other is common.
entries.note: smooth firm not hard; one bigger/lower common

entries.sentence: The NHS says to book a GP appointment for a lump, swelling, change in shape or feel, or an ache that does not go away.
entries.note: see GP for these

entries.sentence: Most lumps have causes other than cancer, such as hydroceles, cysts, varicoceles or epididymitis.
entries.note: most benign; examples

entries.sentence: Sudden, severe testicle pain is an emergency: the NHS says to go to A&E or call 999.
entries.note: torsion emergency; A&E/999

entries.sentence: Testicular cancer is one possible cause, and the NHS says it is easier to treat when found early.
entries.note: cancer rare one possible cause; easier to treat if found early

entries.sentence: The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower.
entries.note: Check during or just after a warm bath or shower; about once a month.

entries.sentence: The testicles sit inside the scrotum, the bag of skin below the penis.
entries.note: plain general knowledge

entries.sentence: To start, hold your scrotum in the palm of your hand.
entries.note: Hold the scrotum in the palm of your hand.

entries.sentence: Then, with your other hand, roll one testicle at a time between your thumb and fingers.
entries.note: Roll one testicle at a time between thumb and fingers.

entries.sentence: The NHS also describes feeling the tubes at the back of each testicle, called the epididymis.
entries.note: Feel the epididymis at the back of each testicle.

entries.sentence: These can sometimes become hard, swollen or painful.
entries.note: Epididymis can sometimes become hard, swollen or painful.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a healthy testicle feels smooth and firm, but not hard.
entries.note: A healthy testicle should feel smooth and firm, but not hard.

entries.sentence: It is common for one testicle to be slightly bigger than the other, or to hang lower.
entries.note: Common for one to be slightly bigger or hang lower.

entries.sentence: This means the most useful thing to learn is what is normal for you.
entries.note: What matters is noticing changes from your own normal.

entries.sentence: Checking regularly makes it easier to notice when something has changed.
entries.note: Regular checking and noticing changes; suggested about once a month.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists several changes to look out for.
entries.note: NHS lists symptoms.

entries.sentence: These include a lump in a testicle, a swollen testicle, or a change in the shape or feel of a testicle.
entries.note: Lump, swelling, change in shape or how they feel.

entries.sentence: One testicle becoming bigger than the other can also be a change worth noting.
entries.note: One testicle becoming bigger than the other.

entries.sentence: So can an ache or pain in a testicle or the scrotum that does not go away.
entries.note: Aching that does not go away; ache or pain in testicle or scrotum.

entries.sentence: A scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard is on the same list.
entries.note: Scrotum feeling heavy, firm or hard.

entries.sentence: The NHS stresses that having these symptoms does not mean you have testicular cancer.
entries.note: Having these symptoms does not mean you have testicular cancer, but it is important to get them checked by a GP.

entries.sentence: The NHS says most lumps and swellings in the testicles turn out to have causes other than cancer.
entries.note: Most testicular lumps are benign.

entries.sentence: It names several common ones, including varicoceles, hydroceles, epididymal cysts and epididymitis.
entries.note: Varicoceles, hydroceles, epididymal cysts, epididymo-orchitis, inguinal hernias, torsion listed.

entries.sentence: It also lists a hernia in the groin as a possible cause.
entries.note: Inguinal hernias listed.

entries.sentence: A hydrocele is a swelling of the scrotum caused by a build-up of fluid.
entries.note: Hydroceles: swelling in the scrotum caused by a build-up of fluid.

entries.sentence: A varicocele is a soft lump that develops slowly above the testicle, usually on the left side.
entries.note: Varicoceles: soft lumps that develop gradually above the testicle and on the left side.

entries.sentence: An epididymal cyst is a small, smooth, fluid-filled swelling that develops slowly in the epididymis.
entries.note: Epididymal cysts: small smooth fluid-filled swelling slowly developing in the epididymis.

entries.sentence: Epididymitis happens when the epididymis becomes swollen and painful, often because of an infection.
entries.note: Epididymitis: epididymis swollen and painful, often due to infection.

entries.sentence: The NHS says it is usually treated with antibiotics.
entries.note: Usually treated with antibiotics.

entries.sentence: It adds that in men under 35 the cause is usually a sexually transmitted infection, while in men over 35 it is more often a urine infection.
entries.note: Under 35 usually an STI such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea; over 35 main cause usually urine infection.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to make a GP appointment if you notice a lump or swelling in a testicle.
entries.note: See GP for lump/swelling (non-urgent appointment).

entries.sentence: The same goes for a change in the shape or feel of a testicle, or one testicle becoming bigger than the other.
entries.note: Change in shape or how they feel; one bigger than the other.

entries.sentence: An ache that does not go away is also a reason to book an appointment.
entries.note: Aching that does not go away.

entries.sentence: This is a routine appointment, not an emergency.
entries.note: Non-urgent GP appointment for these symptoms.

entries.sentence: The NHS still wants these changes checked, even though most turn out not to be cancer.
entries.note: Important to get them checked by a GP.

entries.sentence: A GP can look at and feel the testicles and may arrange an ultrasound scan.
entries.note: The doctor will examine the testicles and may arrange an ultrasound.

entries.sentence: In Scotland, NHS inform adds that a GP may also shine a torch through the scrotum to look for fluid.
entries.note: In Scotland the GP may shine a torch through the scrotum to check for a build-up of fluid.

entries.sentence: Yes, the NHS treats sudden, severe pain in a testicle as an emergency.
entries.note: Sudden severe testicle pain: go to A&E.

entries.sentence: It can be a sign of testicular torsion, where the blood supply to a testicle is cut off.
entries.note: Torsion: blood supply to testicle cut off.

entries.sentence: The NHS says this needs treatment in hospital as soon as possible.
entries.note: Needs hospital treatment as soon as possible; suspected torsion needs emergency surgery.

entries.sentence: The route is to go straight to A&E or call 999, rather than waiting to see a GP.
entries.note: Go straight to A&E or call 999 (NHS 111 Wales); do not wait.

entries.sentence: NHS pages also list pain together with sickness or tummy pain, or pain that lasts more than an hour, as reasons to get emergency help.
entries.note: Pain with sickness or tummy pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest (NHS 111 Wales).

entries.sentence: A swollen scrotum or a testicle sitting higher than usual can also go with torsion.
entries.note: Other features can include swelling of the scrotum, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, a testicle sitting higher than normal.

entries.sentence: Testicular cancer is one possible cause of a lump or swelling, and the NHS describes it as rare.
entries.note: Cancer is rare, but it is one possible cause.

entries.sentence: Its main signs are the same ones described above, such as a lump, swelling, or a heavy, firm or hard scrotum.
entries.note: Symptoms of testicular cancer: lump or swelling, getting bigger, ache or pain, scrotum heavy, firm or hard.

entries.sentence: Most people with these signs will not have cancer, but a GP is the person to check.
entries.note: These symptoms do not mean you have testicular cancer; get them checked by a GP.

entries.sentence: The NHS says testicular cancer is easier to treat when it is found early.
entries.note: Testicular cancer is easier to treat if it is found early.

entries.sentence: This is one reason it encourages men to get to know their own testicles.
entries.note: Regular checking; changes from own normal.

entries.sentence: If a GP is concerned about cancer, the NHS says you may be referred urgently through the fast-track two-week system.
entries.note: If GP is concerned about cancer, referral urgently using fast-track (2-week wait) system.

entries.sentence: Being referred this way does not mean cancer has been found, only that the NHS wants you seen quickly.
entries.note: plain general knowledge
